episode_title: Why every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team | Josh Woodward (Google Labs, Gemini, AI Studio)
description_html:
Josh Woodward is the head of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. He has spent over 17 years at Google and oversees its longest-running and largest labs team, whose products include NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), Project Genie, and Flow. His job is to find, experiment with, and scale new AI products, and he has built one of the most distinctive product cultures in the industry for generating ideas, running experiments, and, even more importantly, knowing when to quit.

In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:

1. Why every company now needs to think and operate like a labs team

2. Where the best ideas really come from

3. The “almost possible” framework

4. How to recognize genuine product-market fit early

5. When to kill an idea

6. What skills are rising in value in the AI era

7. Why roles are not actually blurring into one universal builder role

8. How to set up your internal labs team

—

summary.overview: Josh Woodward, head of Google Labs, Gemini, and AI Studio, argues that every company needs a team operating at the frontier of rapidly changing technology. He explains how Labs finds and tests ideas, recognizes product-market fit, decides when to stop, structures teams, and balances zero-to-one experimentation with scaling products such as NotebookLM, Flow, and AI Studio.

takeaways.heading: Why labs matter
takeaways.detail: Josh agrees that companies need people whose job is to explore the newest models and discover what is possible before competitors do. The challenge is bringing startup-like experimentation into larger organizations without distracting teams focused on existing businesses.

takeaways.heading: Where ideas come from
takeaways.detail: The best ideas rarely emerge from design sprints or scheduled brainstorming; they often arise while people are swimming, walking in hallways, or pursuing side projects. Labs tries to create space for curious, obsessed small teams and stay alert for promising work.

takeaways.heading: Track the frontier
takeaways.detail: Josh recommends maintaining a list of what is “almost possible,” then watching for moments when a technical threshold is crossed. Labs also develops predictions about the future, while accepting that most predictions will be wrong, and looks beyond the Bay Area for changing user behaviors.

takeaways.heading: From technology to value
takeaways.detail: A technical breakthrough is not enough: it must connect to a meaningful user problem and, ideally, something people will pay for. Josh cited the first NotebookLM podcast and early Google Flow prototypes as moments when a new capability felt immediately compelling.

takeaways.heading: Recognizing product-market fit
takeaways.detail: Early on, Josh looks less at DAU, retention, or other standard metrics and more at people’s reactions to prototypes: whether their eyes light up, they lean in, and ask to use the product. Teams should fall in love with the problem rather than a particular solution, since several pivots may be needed.

takeaways.heading: When to stop
takeaways.detail: The team often knows an idea is failing before its leader does. Fading passion, exhausted attempts to make the product work, and weak reactions from users are signals to stop or pivot; leaders should create a culture where teams can say this openly.

takeaways.heading: Labs and Gemini together
takeaways.detail: Although Gemini has more than a billion users and Labs often celebrates 10,000 monthly active users, both attract builders with a zero-to-one mentality. Their shared priority order is “users first, Google second, and our product third.”

takeaways.heading: Consumer opportunities
takeaways.detail: Josh sees major opportunities in immersive entertainment, messaging and chat, and products addressing scarce resources such as time, money, memories, and shared real-world experiences. He is unsure whether future products will look like chatbots, personal agents, super apps, or something else.

takeaways.heading: Personal intelligence
takeaways.detail: Josh said Gemini already offers some connections to Google data through Gemini Spark, and that Google is moving toward a simpler experience in which users describe what they want in one prompt. He described the broader direction as a personal, proactive, powerful Gemini.

takeaways.heading: Under- and overhyped
takeaways.detail: Josh thinks the industry under-discusses the principles and future it is encoding through products. He considers model benchmarks overhyped because most users care about useful products and features, not Elo ratings or benchmark scores.

takeaways.heading: Valuable skills
takeaways.detail: He is watching for “unlearning rate”—how quickly someone can abandon an approach after new evidence—as well as “explosive endurance,” collaboration, and the ability to build trust. He expects people to work with agents and changing groups of colleagues, making collaboration more important rather than less.

takeaways.heading: Specialties still matter
takeaways.detail: Josh does not believe everyone is simply becoming the same kind of builder. People may become broader, but they still retain specialties—their “major”—while building becomes a complementary “minor”; Labs draws effective contributors from PM, design, engineering, strategy, operations, BD, and marketing.

takeaways.heading: Work rhythms
takeaways.detail: Labs organizes work into seasons, explicitly naming periods of intense execution and periods for exploration. After major events such as Google I/O, teams may be encouraged to hack and rediscover what is new rather than ship, while planning generally operates on a rolling six-month horizon with meaningful progress targeted within roughly 50 to 100 days.

takeaways.heading: Designing a labs team
takeaways.detail: Josh recommends giving a Labs team enough independence for unusual ideas to grow, defining whether its role is to graduate ideas into existing products or create new categories, and using it to challenge how the wider company works. He cautioned against hiring too many people too quickly and mistaking headcount growth for progress.

takeaways.heading: Who belongs in Labs
takeaways.detail: Strong Labs candidates build constantly, stay intellectually curious, read and follow new developments, focus on solving users’ problems rather than personal glory, and add energy to conversations. Josh also looks for people energized by uncertain, unstructured problems.

takeaways.heading: Labs stages and rewards
takeaways.detail: Google Labs distinguishes zero-to-one, one-to-ten, and ten-to-a-hundred work because each stage has different goals and metrics. The team uses playful awards—including a TPU Harvester rake, a golden Band-Aid for fixing paper cuts, and large ears for an “LLM Whisperer”—to reinforce valued behaviors.

takeaways.heading: Google’s future shape
takeaways.detail: Asked whether Google will have 10,000 products or five in five years, Josh said he keeps changing his answer and is unsure whether “products” will remain the right unit. Labs is testing both highly consolidated and highly fragmented possibilities, including experiences generated or personalized by models.

takeaways.heading: Better feedback loops
takeaways.detail: Josh sees an open opportunity in using AI to collect and interpret product feedback, surface insights, and help teams understand what will delight particular users. He is also interested in AI helping people collaborate in the way especially insightful colleagues do.
